title: The transformer block
objectives: Build a pre-norm transformer block from attention, a feed-forward net and layer normalisation.

screens.title: Wiring the parts
screens.prose: You have built causal multi-head attention, layer norm and a one-hidden-layer MLP. A **transformer block** chains them. Each of its two parts reads a layer-normalised copy of the vector. Its output is then added back to the vector it read.
screens.question: Put the steps in the order a vector meets them.

lines.text: Causal multi-head attention on the normalised copy
Add the attention output to $\mathbf x$
The MLP on that copy, one position at a time
Add the MLP output to $\mathbf x$

hints.text: Each part reads a normalised copy, so the norm comes just before it.
Attention comes first: LN 1, attention, then the addition.
LN 1, attention, add; then LN 2, MLP, add.

feedback.correct: That is the block: normalise, attend, add; normalise, MLP, add.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Each part comes straight after its own layer norm, and its output is added before the next part reads.

byKey.s3: Add the attention output after the attention has run, before the second layer norm reads the vector.
byKey.s5: The MLP reads the second normalised copy, so LN 2 comes just before it.

explain.text: Wired up, the vector runs along the bottom and each part adds a correction to it. Attention goes first, so the MLP reads a vector that already holds the earlier positions' information.

canvas.caption: The straight line along the bottom is the residual path: $\mathbf x$ reaches the output with the two updates added.

screens.title: A pre-norm block
screens.prose: The block is $\mathbf x \leftarrow \mathbf x + \operatorname{Attn}(\operatorname{LN}_1(\mathbf x))$, then $\mathbf x \leftarrow \mathbf x + \operatorname{MLP}(\operatorname{LN}_2(\mathbf x))$. Normalising before each part makes it **pre-norm**. The MLP widens each position from $d$ to $4d$, applies ReLU, and narrows back to $d$. Take $T = 8$ and $d = 64$.
screens.question: How many numbers does the MLP's hidden layer hold for the whole sequence?

hints.text: The hidden layer is $4d$ wide at every position.
$4 \times 64 = 256$ at each of 8 positions.

feedback.correct: $8 \times 256 = 2{,}048$: 256 hidden units at each of the 8 positions.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the hidden width, then count it at every position.

byKey.one: That is one position. The MLP runs at all 8.
byKey.d: You kept the width at $d$. The hidden layer is $4d$ wide.

explain.text: The hidden layer holds $8 \times 256 = 2{,}048$ numbers; every other step keeps the shape $(T, d)$, which lets the additions work. The width changes back before the addition.

screens.title: One position by hand
screens.prose: One position, $d = 2$, $\mathbf x = (1, 3)$. Layer norms have gain 1 and shift 0; ignore $\epsilon$. With one position the attention weight is 1, so attention returns $\operatorname{LN}_1(\mathbf x)\mathbf W_V\mathbf W_O$, here $\mathbf W_V = \mathbf I$, $\mathbf W_O = 0.5\mathbf I$, with no biases anywhere. The MLP has $\mathbf W_1 = \mathbf I$ and $\mathbf W_2 = 2\mathbf I$.
screens.question: What is the first coordinate of the block's output?

hints.text: Attention adds $0.5 \times (-1, 1)$ to $(1, 3)$.
After attention, $\mathbf x = (0.5, 3.5)$, whose layer norm is again $(-1, 1)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Work down the table: each addition keeps what was there.

byKey.norelu: You skipped the ReLU, so $-1$ passed through and took 2 off the first coordinate.
byKey.replace: You replaced $\mathbf x$ by the MLP output. The block adds it to $\mathbf x$.
byKey.first-add: You dropped $\mathbf x$ at the first addition, so the stream lost the input.

explain.text: The stream goes $(1, 3) \to (0.5, 3.5) \to (0.5, 5.5)$. Each part sees a normalised copy. Its output lands on the raw vector, so the input survives into the output.

screens.title: The MLP in code
screens.prose: Write `mlp_block(x, params)`: $\operatorname{ReLU}(\mathbf x\mathbf W_1 + \mathbf b_1)\mathbf W_2 + \mathbf b_2$, applied to each row of $\mathbf x$. Rows are positions, so one matrix product handles them all. GPT-2 uses GELU, a smooth ReLU; we keep ReLU.
screens.question: Complete `mlp_block`.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np


def mlp_block(x, params):
    h = np.maximum(0, np.asarray(x, dtype=float) @ params['W1'] + params['b1'])
    return h @ params['W2'] + params['b2']

screens.title: Mixing the positions
screens.prose: A colleague writes the MLP as $\operatorname{ReLU}(\mathbf A\mathbf X)\mathbf W$, with $\mathbf A$ an 8 by 8 matrix. It acts along the position axis of $\mathbf X$ ($T = 8$). It trains, and the training loss falls fast.
screens.question: What has gone wrong?

options.text: Every output row now mixes all 8 positions, later ones too, so the model reads ahead and fits only length 8
Nothing: attention mixes positions too, so a second mixing step is harmless
options.why: Attention mixes positions under the causal mask. $\mathbf A$ has no mask, so position 0 reads position 7.

options.text: Only the cost: it is the same layer with more weights
options.why: It is a different layer. Rows that were independent now depend on each other.

hints.text: Which positions does output row 0 depend on?
Row 0 of $\mathbf A\mathbf X$ is a mix of all 8 rows of $\mathbf X$.
Position 0 sees position 7: the mask is broken.

feedback.correct: Right: the falling loss is the model reading the answer from later positions.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what row 0 of $\mathbf A\mathbf X$ depends on.

byKey.fine: You trusted the mask to cover it. Only attention is masked; this matrix reaches every position.
byKey.cost: You counted weights only. The layer's outputs now depend on other positions.

explain.text: In a block, attention mixes positions (under the mask) and the MLP mixes features of one position. Mixing positions inside the MLP leaks the future and ties the model to one length.

def transformer_block(x, params, h):

    # Attention: project with Wq, bq, Wk, bk, Wv, bv; split into h heads; causal attention; merge; Wo, bo.
    # The ops take and return Tensors: use .data for the array.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np
from nt_ops_l2 import layernorm
from seq_ops_l3 import attention, causal_mask, merge_heads, split_heads


def transformer_block(x, params, h):
    p = params
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    T = x.shape[-2]
    a = layernorm(x, p['ln1_g'], p['ln1_b'])
    q, k, v = (split_heads(a @ p[w] + p[b], h) for w, b in (('Wq', 'bq'), ('Wk', 'bk'), ('Wv', 'bv')))
    att = merge_heads(attention(q, k, v, causal_mask(T))) @ p['Wo'] + p['bo']
    x = x + att.data
    m = layernorm(x, p['ln2_g'], p['ln2_b'])
    return x + ((m @ p['W1'] + p['b1']).relu() @ p['W2'] + p['b2']).data
widget.prelude:
import numpy as np


def planted(d, dm, seed):
    g = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    p = {}
    for k in ('Wq', 'Wk', 'Wv', 'Wo'):
        p[k] = g.standard_normal((d, d)) / np.sqrt(d)
    p['W1'] = g.standard_normal((d, dm)) / np.sqrt(d)
    p['W2'] = g.standard_normal((dm, d)) / np.sqrt(dm)
    for k, n in (('bq', d), ('bk', d), ('bv', d), ('bo', d), ('b1', dm), ('b2', d), ('ln1_b', d), ('ln2_b', d)):
        p[k] = 0.1 * g.standard_normal(n)
    p['ln1_g'] = 1 + 0.2 * g.standard_normal(d)
    p['ln2_g'] = 1 + 0.2 * g.standard_normal(d)
    return p


PB = planted(8, 32, 3)
X6 = np.random.default_rng(5).standard_normal((6, 8)) * 2 + 1

import numpy as np
from nt_ops_l2 import layernorm
from seq_ops_l3 import attention, causal_mask, merge_heads, split_heads


def transformer_block(x, params, h):
    p = params
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    T = x.shape[-2]
    a = x
    q, k, v = (split_heads(a @ p[w] + p[b], h) for w, b in (('Wq', 'bq'), ('Wk', 'bk'), ('Wv', 'bv')))
    att = merge_heads(attention(q, k, v, causal_mask(T))) @ p['Wo'] + p['bo']
    x = layernorm(x + att.data, p['ln1_g'], p['ln1_b']).data
    m = x

import numpy as np
from nt_ops_l2 import layernorm
from seq_ops_l3 import attention, causal_mask, merge_heads, split_heads


def transformer_block(x, params, h):
    p = params
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    T = x.shape[-2]
    a = layernorm(x, p['ln1_g'], p['ln1_b'])
    q, k, v = (split_heads(a @ p[w] + p[b], h) for w, b in (('Wq', 'bq'), ('Wk', 'bk'), ('Wv', 'bv')))
    att = merge_heads(attention(q, k, v, None)) @ p['Wo'] + p['bo']
    x = x + att.data
    m = layernorm(x, p['ln2_g'], p['ln2_b'])
    return x + ((m @ p['W1'] + p['b1']).relu() @ p['W2'] + p['b2']).data

screens.title: Before or after the addition
screens.prose: Vaswani et al. (2017) normalised after each addition: $\mathbf x \leftarrow \operatorname{LN}(\mathbf x + \operatorname{Attn}(\mathbf x))$, called **post-norm**. GPT-2 and most models since normalise before each part, as we do.
screens.question: Follow the path from a block's output back to its input. What does post-norm put on it that pre-norm leaves off?

options.text: A layer norm after each addition, so no plain identity path
The causal mask on the attention scores
options.why: Both forms mask attention in the same way.

options.text: Nothing: the two compute the same function
options.why: They differ: where the norm sits changes what each block outputs.

options.text: A second MLP after the first one
options.why: Both have one MLP per block.

hints.text: Trace $\mathbf x$ along the addition only.
In post-norm the sum goes through LN before it leaves the block.
Pre-norm's main path is additions only.

feedback.correct: Right: pre-norm keeps a clean identity path from the last block to the first.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare what sits on the main path in each row.

byKey.same: Move a norm and you change the function: post-norm rescales the sum itself.

explain.text: With pre-norm, $\mathbf x$ passes every block through additions only, so its gradient reaches early blocks directly. That is a likely reason deep pre-norm stacks need less care over warm-up (Xiong et al., 2020). Post-norm can still train well with tuning.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask which step reads more than one row.

byKey.causal: That is the full block: attention would carry the change to positions 3 to 7. With attention removed, nothing does.
byKey.all: No step here reads other rows, and even attention would not reach back to rows 0 to 2.

explain.text: Without attention the block is a per-position MLP with a skip, so 1 row changes: row 3. Attention is the only part that moves information between positions.

screens.title: The transformer block
screens.prose: A pre-norm block of width $d$ computes $$\mathbf x \leftarrow \mathbf x + \operatorname{Attn}(\operatorname{LN}_1(\mathbf x)), \qquad \mathbf x \leftarrow \mathbf x + \operatorname{MLP}(\operatorname{LN}_2(\mathbf x)),$$ with the MLP $d \to 4d \to d$ on each position. Both parts keep the shape $(T, d)$, so blocks stack.
screens.question: Which part of the block moves information from one position to another?

options.why: The MLP acts on each row alone: it mixes features of one position.
Layer norm rescales each position by its own mean and spread.
An addition adds a part's output at the same position.

feedback.correct: Right: attention mixes positions; the MLP mixes features.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which step reads more than one row?

explain.text: Attention is the one step that reads other rows, and the mask limits it to earlier ones. Everything else acts row by row, so a block's leaks can only come from attention.

ideas: A pre-norm block computes $\mathbf x + \operatorname{Attn}(\operatorname{LN}_1(\mathbf x))$, then adds $\operatorname{MLP}(\operatorname{LN}_2(\mathbf x))$; every step keeps the shape $(T, d)$.
Attention mixes positions under the causal mask; the MLP ($d \to 4d \to d$, ReLU here, GELU in GPT-2) mixes the features of each position alone.
Post-norm (Vaswani et al., 2017) normalises after each addition; pre-norm keeps a plain identity path through every block.

formula.tex: \mathbf x \leftarrow \mathbf x + \operatorname{Attn}(\operatorname{LN}_1(\mathbf x)),\quad \mathbf x \leftarrow \mathbf x + \operatorname{MLP}(\operatorname{LN}_2(\mathbf x))
formula.note: Each part reads a normalised copy and writes back by addition.
